Do not present a mitigation as a security control unless it actually enforces a trust boundary, and never let untrusted input influence code that runs with privileged credentials. Before documenting or shipping a feature as "security," verify it can't be trivially bypassed; if it can, describe it only as a convenience/filtering mechanism (e.g., "skip minified build output") rather than a safeguard. In automated pipelines, treat anything checked out from an external or untrusted source (such as a pull request) as hostile: if a job exposes secrets (e.g., `GH_TOKEN`) to hooks/plugins/scripts, those scripts must not be loaded from the checked-out, attacker-controllable tree. Either avoid checking out untrusted content when secrets are present (e.g., diff the PR with `gh pr diff` against the base branch instead of checking it out), explicitly remove untrusted config/hook directories before the privileged step runs, or enforce controls only via global, non-repo-controlled hooks. Finally, when generated artifacts can contain secrets (API keys, tokens, cached credentials), ensure exclusion rules (e.g., `.gitignore`) use recursive patterns (`**/path/`) rather than root-anchored ones, and verify coverage with tools like `git check-ignore` so secrets committed from nested subfolders are still caught.
